Question: 1. Consider your community- and facility-based health education activities, aimed at both young and adult women, and their partners. Are these activities conducted to increase awareness about (a) the advantages and (b) the availability of the following services to:
column2: support informed decision-making about sexual debut, the risks of HIV transmission and the use of contraception, including condoms?
support consistent use of male or female condoms to prevent HIV transmission, other STIs, and unintended pregnancy?
encourage uptake of voluntary counselling and testing in order to determine their HIV status?
encourage the early treatment of sexually transmitted infections?

Question: 2. Are these activities and services provided in an adolescent- or youth-friendly manner? Do they attempt to address – even in a partial way – the structural factors that increase women’s vulnerability to HIV, such as:
column2: gender inequality?
multiple concurrent partnerships?
violence against women?
HIV-related stigma and discrimination?

Question: 3. Are women who have experienced gender-based violence routinely provided with:
column2: counselling support and related SRH services?
psychosocial and legal support?
emergency contraception in the event of a sexual assault?
post-exposure prophylaxis in the event of a sexual assault?

Question: 4. For those women who are pregnant, have tested HIV-negative and are attending antenatal, or post-partum care services, are they routinely:
column2: provided with information and counselling on safer sex, risk reduction and condom use during the course of their pregnancy and the post-partum period?
provided with information and counselling on STI prevention (including information on the recognition of symptoms) and, where necessary, the treatment of STIs?
encouraged and supported to involve their male partner in their antenatal and post-natal care consultations?
provided with the contraceptives of choice in preparation for post-partum sexual activity and, importantly, provided with condoms during their antenatal care consultations?

provided with an opportunity to discuss the issue of post-partum sexual activity and contraception early after delivery or even late in the last trimester to provide women with the appropriate knowledge to allow them to make informed decisions regarding their reproductive futures?
encouraged to re-test for HIV on a regular basis throughout and after their pregnancy – ideally with their partner in the context of a couple counselling session?

Question: 5. Are contraceptive commodities and, importantly, male and female condoms, readily available to women at every consultation they have with a health service provider?
6. Are creative strategies used by health care providers to encourage greater male involvement in antenatal, maternity and post-partum care such as:
column2: educational talks?
an invitation to attend a medical consultation without waiting in line?
couple counselling?

Question: 7. Are health care providers, with a woman’s consent, able to skilfully address male partners in such a way as to raise awareness of their responsibility for practising safer sex and facilitate the associated behaviour change?

column2: are all members of the health team sufficiently trained to provide the above interventions with their clients?

has the team agreed at which points in the PMTCT process (i.e. provider-initiated HIV testing and counselling, antenatal care, intrapartum care, post-natal care, and follow-up of HIV-exposed infants) the above information and counselling will be provided to clients?
has the health team identified which members of the health team will provide clients with the above information and services?

are the above elements incorporated into standard operating procedures or guidelines of the facility or organization, so that all (and specifically new) members of the health team are aware of this practice?
